1:
The chapter opens with a date on which no two expositors settle, and the disagreement matters because it decides how far the reforms stand from the dedication of the wall. Gill rules out the obvious reading: this was not when the wall was dedicated, nor soon after, since it cannot be thought that the people were corrupted so quickly; it belongs rather to the time after Nehemiah had governed twelve years, had been at Babylon, and had returned. Wesley reads it the same way, placing it on a certain day after Nehemiah's return from the Persian court, from which he had been absent for a considerable time during which errors and abuses had crept in. Henry takes the other side, and takes it almost at face value: the law happened to be read on that day, as it should seem the day of the dedication of the wall, since with their prayers and praises the people joined the reading of the word. He concedes an alternative — that it may have been the anniversary commemoration of that day some years later, and is therefore called that day — and he distinguishes this grievance from the rest, since the mixed multitude could be put away by the people's own act, whereas the other abuses waited to be redressed by Nehemiah's power.

What the reading uncovered is a standing exclusion, and Henry frames it as a matter of Israel's vocation rather than of policy. It was the honour of Israel and the greatest preservation of their holiness that they were a peculiar people, bound to keep themselves so, not to mingle with the nations nor to let any of them be incorporated. What they found written was that Ammonites and Moabites should not be naturalised, should not settle among them, nor unite with them. Wesley glosses the phrase about not coming in to the same effect: not to be incorporated into the commonwealth of Israel, nor joined with any Israelite in marriage.

Henry also draws out what the occasion shows about public reading, and makes it the chapter's opening principle. See the benefit of the public reading of the word of God: when it is duly attended to, it discovers to us sin and duty, good and evil, and shows us where we have erred. And he adds the test of profit — we profit by that discovery only when it works upon us to separate ourselves from the evil we had addicted ourselves to.

Gill locates the chapter's starting point in Nehemiah's own movements rather than in the calendar, and the two accounts of the date are left standing side by side: either the law was read at the dedication and the people acted at once, with the rest of the reforms following years later, or the whole chapter belongs to the second governorship, after the twelve years and the journey to Babylon. The witnesses who date it late have the state of the people on their side; Henry, who dates the reading early, has the narrative's own phrase.
2:
The law's reason is given before its application, and Henry treats the reason as the point. The Ammonites and Moabites were excluded because they had been injurious and ill-natured to the Israel of God: they had not shown them common civility but had sought their ruin, though Israel not only did them no harm but was expressly forbidden to do them any. He locates the statute with its reason in Deuteronomy, and Gill refers the reader to the same place, noting that the identical ground is given there. The two halves of the reason are of different kinds — a refusal of bread and water, which is a failure of hospitality, and the hiring of Balaam, which is an attempt at destruction — and the verse sets them together as one indictment.

The clause about the curse turned into a blessing is the verse's own comment on that attempt, and it is what makes the exclusion a matter of history rather than of grudge. The hire was paid, the prophet was brought, and the imprecation he was engaged to pronounce came out the other way; the people excluded here are excluded as those whose enmity God had already overruled once.

What the people did on hearing is told in a single sentence, and who exactly was put away is read three ways. Keil and Delitzsch work on the term rendered mixed multitude: it is the word used of the non-Israelitish crowd that followed Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 12:38), transferred here to strangers of various heathen nationalities living among the people, and once the law was understood all such strangers were separated from Israel. Clarke reads the separation more concretely and more severely: they excluded all strange women, and all persons young and old who had been born of these illegal connections. Wesley takes the phrase for all the heathen people with whom Israel had contracted alliance, which puts the emphasis on the alliances rather than on the descent.

Gill supplies what had been heard — the law concerning the Ammonite and the Moabite, which by extension reached other nations and forbade marriage with them — and so reads the compliance as going beyond the letter of what was read. Henry draws the lesson from the promptness. These inmates the people expelled as usurpers and dangerous, and he recalls that the mixed multitude had of old been a snare to Israel, since it was the mixed multitude that fell a-lusting in the wilderness. Keil and Delitzsch add a caution about the date: the occurrence cannot be more precisely fixed from the phrase about that day, since public readings of the law were frequent in those days.
4:
The narrative turns back to explain how the abuse arose, and the commentators begin with the identity of the man responsible. Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch both take Eliashib for the high priest. Ellicott agrees, identifying him with the Eliashib of the earlier chapter and noting that the office alone would not have given him control over the chambers — the series of rooms running round three walls of the temple — so the oversight must have been a particular charge. He adds a telling observation from silence: there is a suspicious absence of Eliashib's name throughout the high religious festivities of the preceding chapters. Clarke is less sure, allowing that this may have been a different person from the high priest while conceding there is no indubitable evidence that he was not the same; and if he was the high priest, Clarke says, he was very unfaithful to the charge he had received and a reproach to the priesthood.

How the alliance came about is traced through a marriage. Clarke reports that Eliashib had married his grandson to Sanballat's daughter, which produced the connection with Tobiah, Sanballat's fast friend, and in Tobiah's favour he polluted the house of God. Henry presses the scandal harder and from the law. It was expressly provided that the high priest should marry one of his own people, or else he profanes his seed among his people; and for Eliashib to contract an alliance with an Ammonite — a servant, for so Tobiah is called — and then to value himself upon it, probably because the man was cried up as a fine gentleman, was such a contempt of the crown of his consecration as one would not wish told in Gath. Wesley identifies Tobiah plainly as the Ammonite and a violent enemy to God's people.

The chamber itself is the measure of the favour. Gill and Ellicott both explain that the great chamber was made by throwing several smaller ones together, and Wesley fills in the method and the motive: by removing the things out of it, uniting divers small chambers into one, and furnishing it for Tobiah's use when he came to Jerusalem, Eliashib seems to have lodged him there so as to have freer communication with him. Keil and Delitzsch describe it as a large chamber in the fore-court of the temple, probably for Tobiah's use as a dwelling when he visited the city.

What was displaced to make room is what the witnesses find worst. The verse itself lists it — the meat offerings, the frankincense, the vessels, the tithes of corn and new wine and oil commanded to be given to the Levites and the singers and the porters, and the offerings of the priests. Henry enumerates four separate wrongs in the arrangement: that an Ammonite should be entertained with respect in Israel at all; that the high priest, who should have taught the people the law, should contrary to the law provide the entertainment and use his power over the temple chambers to do it; that he should lodge him in the courts of God's house, which Henry reckons next to setting up an idol there; and that he should throw out the temple stores to make room, exposing the priests' portions to be wasted and embezzled merely to gratify Tobiah. Thus, Henry says, did he corrupt the covenant of Levi, as Malachi was complaining at that very time.
6:
Nehemiah interrupts his own narrative to say where he was, and the commentators treat the parenthesis as the explanation of everything in the preceding verses. Gill puts it simply: he was absent all the while these things were done by Eliashib, or otherwise they would not have been suffered. Wesley says the same from the other side, that Eliashib took the occasion of his absence to do these things. Ellicott calls the clause a parenthetical explanation of the disorderly state of affairs, and Henry reaches for the pattern behind it — the envious one who sows tares in God's field knows how to take his opportunity when the servants sleep or are absent, and the golden calf was made while Moses was in the mount. Nothing, Henry adds, grieves a good magistrate more than to see the ministers of God's house do a wicked thing.

The chronology is worked out from the regnal year. Clarke sets out the whole sequence: Nehemiah came to Jerusalem in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes and remained twelve years until the thirty-second, then returned to Babylon and stayed a year, obtained leave to revisit his brethren, and found matters as this chapter states them. Ellicott derives the same interval from the text, observing that the thirty-second year shows he had been in Jerusalem twelve years before returning to the king, and he notes that the phrase about certain days leaves the length of the second absence indefinite.

One detail of the title draws comment. Ellicott observes that Nehemiah calls Artaxerxes king of Babylon rather than king of Persia, and suggests the reason is simply that it was at Babylon that he found the court. Wesley reads the verb of coming as going from Jerusalem to the king rather than arriving, since Nehemiah had been at the court more than once.

The return and the discovery are told in one movement. Gill notes that he came to Jerusalem through the king's leave and with a commission from him. Keil and Delitzsch describe him as directing his attention on arrival to the evil Eliashib had committed in preparing a chamber in the court of the temple for Tobiah, and they treat the whole passage as Nehemiah reforming the irregularities that had broken out during his absence. Henry supplies how he learned of it — the good people who were troubled at it informed him what an intimacy had grown up between their chief priest and their chief enemy — and what it cost him to hear: it grieved him sorely that God's house should be profaned, his enemies caressed and trusted, and his cause betrayed by the man who should have been its protector and patron.
8:
Nehemiah's own feeling is recorded before his action, and each expositor is careful about what exactly grieved him. Gill refers it to the conversion of a sacred place to common use, and to the use of a heathen and an enemy of the Jews and their religion. Wesley itemises the aggravations: the man who polluted the place ought in several respects not to have come there at all, being no priest, a stranger, an Ammonite, and one of the worst of that people — and all of it done by the permission and order of the high priest. Ellicott counts this the second time we read of Nehemiah's deep emotion, and gives it two grounds: the utter dissoluteness of which the arrangement was a token, and the fact that the desecration was a priestly one.

The action itself is swift and physical, and two witnesses find a precedent for it. Keil and Delitzsch report that he cast out all Tobiah's household stuff and commanded the chamber to be purified and the vessels of the house of God brought back into it, and they draw an inference from the word for household stuff — that Tobiah used the chamber as a dwelling when he came from time to time to Jerusalem. Clarke sets the act beside the cleansing of the temple courts, when the tables of the moneychangers and the seats of those who sold doves were overthrown. Henry presses the same comparison and then turns it inward, noting that Nehemiah did not seize the goods for his own use but cast them out, so that Tobiah, probably absent at the time, should find no conveniences for his reception on returning; and that those who would expel sin from their hearts, those living temples, must likewise throw out its household stuff and all the provision made for it, strip it, starve it, and take away the food and fuel of lust, which is in effect to mortify it.

Henry also marks what the act cost in prudence. Nehemiah did not fear to disoblige Tobiah, nor the resentment of Eliashib, nor did he excuse himself from interposing in an affair that lay within the high priest's jurisdiction; he had power and would use it for God.

The cleansing is treated as a formal matter rather than a tidying. Gill observes that the plural shows there was more than one chamber, or that several had been thrown into one, and that since the uncleanness was ceremonial — contracted by a heathen's dwelling in them — the purification may have been by the water of separation. Keil and Delitzsch list what was brought back, the vessels with the meat offering and the frankincense, and suppose the tenths and heave-offerings also, the enumeration here being abbreviated. Ellicott notices what is absent and calls it a note of minute accuracy: there is no mention of tithes being brought back as yet, and the following verses show why. Henry reads the sequence as a pattern — when sin is cast out of the heart by repentance, let the blood of Christ be applied to it by faith, and then let it be furnished with the graces of God's Spirit for every good work.
10:
The next grievance is a failure of payment, and responsibility for the failure is assigned differently. Henry is precise about what the complaint is not: it is not that the dues were uncollected from the people but that they were not given to the Levites — and the Levites were so modest as not to sue for them. He suspects that Tobiah, on taking possession of the store-chambers, seized the stores too and by Eliashib's connivance converted them to his own use. Wesley sets out both possibilities without choosing: either the corrupt high priest took their portions as he took the chambers, to his own use or for the entertainment of Tobiah and his other great allies; or else the people withheld them, whether out of covetousness and against their own solemn agreement, or because they were so offended at Eliashib's abuse of sacred things that they abhorred the offering and service of God and would not bring in tithes they knew would be perverted. Gill offers a third reading of the same kind, that the tithes having been removed elsewhere might be converted to another use, or that the people seeing what Eliashib had done neglected to bring them in, judging they would not be properly disposed of.

What the Levites did about it is stated plainly and read as a consequence. Keil and Delitzsch summarise that the payment of dues and the delivery of tenths and first-fruits had alike been omitted, so that the Levites and singers who had the work to do had fled each to his field. Ellicott explains the mechanism: those who performed the temple's work were obliged to seek their sustenance by cultivating the fields apportioned to them in the Levitical cities. Clarke states the result and fixes the blame — they were obliged to abandon the sacred service and betake themselves to cultivating the land for their support, and this was the fault of the rulers, who permitted all these abuses.

Henry weighs the clause about the fields in two directions and prefers the second. It may come in as the reason why the payments were withheld: the Levites were non-residents, at their farms in the country when they should have been about the temple, so the people were little inclined to give them their maintenance — and from that he draws a caution for ministers, that if they have not the encouragement they should have, let them consider whether they are not themselves accessory to the contempt they are under by neglecting their business. But he thinks it rather the reason why Nehemiah so quickly perceived that their dues had been denied, because he missed them from their posts and asked where the singers were.

From that Henry draws the chapter's sharpest working maxim, and it cuts both ways. A scandalous maintenance makes a scandalous ministry; the work is neglected because the workmen are. He adds the detail that makes the collapse worse rather than better: it was not long since the payment of the singers' salaries had been put into a very good method, and yet it had failed for want of being looked after.
11:
Nehemiah goes first to the rulers rather than to the people, and on the propriety of that there is no dispute. Keil and Delitzsch explain why: it was the duty of the heads of the community to see that the tithes were regularly brought to the house of God, so the rebuke falls on them. Gill takes the rulers to be the ecclesiastical ones, the priests appointed over those chambers, and says he expostulated with them warmly and chid them severely for their conduct. Wesley reads it the same way, as a sharp reproof of the priests to whom the management of these things was committed, for neglect of their duty and breach of their late solemn promise. Ellicott points to that promise directly, the express covenant of the earlier chapter, and adds a different culprit: the rich men had taken advantage of Nehemiah's absence to indulge their covetousness.

The question Nehemiah puts is read as a quotation turned back on the hearers. Clarke makes the point exactly: they had all solemnly promised that they would never forsake the house of their God, and Nehemiah uses their own words here by way of reproof — alas, he says, how soon is this forgotten. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the charge as meaning that the house was forsaken through the non-delivery of the dues, and note that the rebuke made the impression desired. Wesley enlarges the indictment to cover both parties injured: you have not only wronged men by withholding their dues, but you have occasioned the neglect of God's house and service.

Henry holds the rulers to a standard he thinks generally binding. It is required of magistrates that they use their power to oblige ministers to do their duty and people to do theirs, and Nehemiah accordingly began with the rulers and called them to account — why did you not take notice of this and prevent it? He traces the chain of defaults: the people forsook the Levites, which the law expressly forbade, and then the Levites forsook their post in the house of God; and ministers and people who forsake religion, and magistrates who do not what they can to keep them to it, will all have a great deal to answer for.

The remedy is described in a single verb that the witnesses find worth pausing on. Keil and Delitzsch report that Nehemiah assembled the Levites and set them in their place, and Ellicott that they were summoned back from their fields; Wesley says gathered to Jerusalem from their several country possessions, and restored to the exercise of their office. Henry renders the phrase as setting them in their stations and draws the figure out — a Levite in his field is out of his station, since God's house is his place and there let him be found. He adds an observation about how little it took: many who are careless would do much better than they do if they were but called upon.
12:
The people's response follows the Levites' restoration rather than any fresh command, and every witness notices the order. Gill explains the change of mind: when they saw a reformation made and things going in their proper channel, so that a right use would be made of their tithes and these given to proper persons now reinstated in their office, they brought them. Wesley gives two motives together, the respect they had to Nehemiah and their seeing that the dues would now be applied to their proper uses. Henry draws the principle out and states it as a rule of church economy: Nehemiah's zeal provoked theirs, and when they saw the Levites at their work they could not for shame withhold their wages any longer, but brought them in honestly and cheerfully. The better church-work is done, he concludes, the better will church-dues be paid.

The second half of the remedy is administrative, and the witnesses treat the organisation as what made the reform stick. Ellicott puts it plainly: the reform was made effectual by organisation. Eliashib had failed in his duty, and the appointment of treasurers made earlier is now confirmed. Gill notes that these were new treasurers, the previously appointed ones being either dead or unfaithful to their trust. Keil and Delitzsch read the verb as a denominative formation meaning to set someone over the treasures, and leave open whether the men named are to be identified with others of the same names elsewhere.

Who was chosen is the point on which the comment turns. Ellicott observes that one of the treasurers was a layman, that all were faithful men mentioned in connection with the building of the wall, and that since the majority were priests and Levites they distributed to their brethren. Clarke renders the reason for their appointment as a report rather than a reputation — they were reported to Nehemiah as persons in whom he could confide, having been steady in God's ways and work while others had been careless and relaxed. Wesley says they were accounted faithful by the consent of those who knew them, and gives the reason Nehemiah sought such men out the more diligently: he had experience of the perfidiousness of the former trustees.

Henry makes the appointment a case of a general maxim about trust. Commissioners were appointed, and they were such as had been accounted faithful — that is, had approved themselves so in other trusts committed to them, and so had purchased to themselves a good degree. Let men be tried first and then trusted, he says, tried in the less and then trusted with more. Their office he describes as to receive and to pay, distributing to their brethren in due season and due proportions, which is the whole of what the earlier arrangement had failed to do.
14:
Nehemiah breaks off to pray, and the commentators are unanimous that the prayer is not a claim. Gill states the distinction first: he asks to be remembered not in a way of strict justice, as though he thought he merited anything at God's hand for what he had done, but in a way of grace and mercy — that God would graciously accept it as done for the honour of His name and overlook all the failings and infirmities in it. Ellicott reads it the same way, as the faithful servant of God once more begging a merciful remembrance of what he had done for the honour of God in the observances of His temple. Clarke turns the request into an argument against itself and then back again: if God were strict to mark what is done amiss, even his good deeds must be wiped out; so the petition becomes, Lord, remember me in thy mercy, and let my upright conduct be acceptable to thee.

Henry examines the two halves of the sentence and finds the restraint in both. The looking back is a matter of satisfaction rather than of merit — it pleased Nehemiah to think that he had been in any way instrumental in reviving and supporting religion in his country and in reforming what was amiss; and Henry generalises it, that whatever kindness any show to God's ministers shall be returned into their own bosoms in the secret joy of having not only done well but done good, good to many and good to souls. The looking up he is careful to distinguish from boasting: Nehemiah refers it to God to consider him for it, not in pride, nor depending on it as his righteousness, nor as though he had made God a debtor, but in a humble appeal concerning his integrity and honest intention, and in a believing expectation that God would not be unrighteous to forget his work and labour of love.

The modesty of the wording is what Henry dwells on longest, and he makes it the measure of the prayer. Observe how modest he is in his requests: he prays only remember me, not reward me; wipe not out my good deeds, not publish them or record them. And then the reversal — yet he was rewarded, and his good deeds were recorded, for God does more than we are able to ask.

What counts as a good deed is defined by the verse itself, and Henry presses the definition. Deeds done for the house of God and the offices of it, for the support of religion and the encouragement of it, are good deeds; there is both righteousness and godliness in them, and God will certainly remember them and not wipe them out, so that they shall in no wise lose their reward. Keil and Delitzsch add only the scope of the clause, that the good deeds are specified as done for the house of God and for the offices thereof, which ties the prayer to the particular reform just described rather than to Nehemiah's career at large.
15:
A new abuse is introduced, and Henry treats the subject itself as the measure of the rest. Nehemiah revived sabbath-sanctification and maintained the authority of the fourth commandment, and Henry calls that a good deed for the house of God and its offices, since where holy time is overlooked and made nothing of it is not strange if all holy duties are neglected. He states it more strongly still: religion is never in the throne while sabbaths are trodden under foot. What makes the discovery worse is where it was made — a general profanation of that holy day even in Jerusalem, that holy city, so lately dedicated to God. Ellicott locates the worst of it in the country, where Nehemiah marked the most determined profanation, and notes that it reached into Jerusalem too, since all kinds of burdens were carried in on that day as on others.

How Nehemiah came to know is itself remarked on. Henry observes that his own eyes were his informers, and draws the rule from it: magistrates who are in care to discharge their duty aright will as far as may be see with their own eyes, and will make diligent search to find out what is evil. Clarke states the finding at its bluntest — the sabbath appears to have been totally disregarded. Keil and Delitzsch date the discovery to the period when Nehemiah was occupied with the arrangements just described, so that the one reform ran into the next.

The particular breaches are itemised, and in each case the witnesses point to a statute that had anticipated it. Henry notes that the husbandmen trod their winepresses and brought home their corn although there was an express command that in earing-time and in harvest they should rest (Exodus 34:21) — a command given, he suggests, precisely because at those seasons men might be tempted to take greater liberty and to fancy that God would indulge them in it. The carriers, he continues, loaded their asses with all manner of burdens and made no scruple of it, though the law had provided for the cattle's rest (Deuteronomy 5:14) and the prophet had forbidden bearing a burden on that day (Jeremiah 17:21). Gill adds the test by which the first of these fails: treading winepresses was not a work of necessity, and so did not, as the Jews express it, drive away the sabbath, since it might have been deferred to another day.

Nehemiah's first step is testimony rather than punishment, and Henry makes the order deliberate. He testified against those who profaned it, not merely expressing his own dislike but endeavouring to convince them that it was a great sin and showing them the testimony of the word of God against it; he would not punish the offence, Henry says, until he had laid open its evil. Keil and Delitzsch summarise the outcome of the whole section in a phrase — field-work and trading on the sabbath done away with — which is the end Nehemiah reaches, but only after the reasoning that follows.
16:
Foreign traders are named next, and the first question is whether they lived in the city or only visited it. The received rendering has them dwelling there, and Gill takes it so, placing their houses or lodgings near the fish gate or fish market where they sold; he traces the fish itself from Tyre and Zidon and the parts adjacent, brought by way of Joppa and from there up to Jerusalem. Keil and Delitzsch dissent on the verb. Most expositors translate it to dwell, they grant, but it is improbable that Tyrians would at that time settle at Jerusalem, so they take the word in its other sense — to sit, that is, to stay awhile undisturbed, to tarry. Ellicott stands between the two: these were the people who had brought timber for the building of the temple and received food in payment (Ezra 3:7), and they now seem to have established themselves as a colony, supplying fish especially to the inhabitants.

Whatever their standing, there is one mind about where the offence lies, and it is not in the trade. Ellicott puts it exactly: their offence was the doing of this on the sabbath, to the children of Judah, and in Jerusalem — and he notes that the verse closes emphatically on that last phrase. Wesley develops the aggravation the place supplies: Jerusalem was the holy city, where God's house was and where the great judicatories of the nation sat, so that the thing was done with manifest contempt of God and of man alike.

Henry turns the attention from the sellers to the buyers, which is where he thinks the guilt chiefly rests. The hawkers and pedlars and petty chapmen were men of Tyre, that famous trading city, and they sold all manner of wares on the sabbath day; but the children of Judah and Jerusalem had so little grace as to buy of them, and so to encourage them in making our Father's day a day of merchandise — contrary to the fourth commandment, which forbids the doing of any manner of work.

From that Henry draws the connection that governs the rest of the chapter. No wonder, he says, that there was a general decay of religion and corruption of manners among this people, when they forsook the sanctuary and profaned the sabbath: the two neglects go together, and the second explains the first. The verse thus serves less as a complaint about Tyrian fishmongers than as evidence of what the people of the city had become willing to buy, and from whom, on the one day they had been given as a sign.
17:
Nehemiah again addresses the rulers rather than the offenders, and the witnesses explain why the charge lands where it does. Gill identifies these nobles as the rulers of the city, the civil magistrates, sharply reproved for their neglect of duty. Clarke states the ground in a line: these evils took place through their negligence, and this he proved before them. Ellicott agrees that the nobles had been responsible in Nehemiah's absence and that the sin is therefore charged upon them. Wesley is most explicit about the mechanism — they are charged with it because, although others did it, it was done by their countenance or connivance, and probably by their example too.

Henry works that out at length and makes it the verse's principal lesson. The charge is you do it, and Henry grants at once that the nobles neither carried corn nor sold fish; what they did was to connive at those who did, not using their power to restrain them, and so making themselves guilty, as magistrates do who bear the sword in vain. They also set a bad example in other things: if the nobles allowed themselves sports and recreations, idle visits and idle talk on the sabbath day, then the men of business in city and country would profane it by their worldly employments as the more justifiable of the two — a point Wesley makes in almost the same terms. From this Henry states the principle plainly: we must be responsible for the sins which others are led to commit by our example.

That the rebuke went to the greatest men first is itself treated as deliberate. Henry observes that the greatest of men are not too high to be told of their faults by those whose proper office it is to reprove them, and goes further — great men should be contended with in the first place, precisely because of the influence they have upon others. He also classifies the offence as the verse does, as an evil thing, proceeding from a great contempt of God and of our own souls.

The argument Nehemiah actually uses is historical, and two witnesses trace it. Keil and Delitzsch report that he reminded the nobles how their forefathers by such acts had brought great evil upon the people and the city — the misery of their former exile and their present oppression — and that he added a warning in the present tense, that by profaning the sabbath they were only increasing the wrath already lying upon Israel. Ellicott notes what the appeal presupposes: their familiarity with the express prediction of Jeremiah and with its literal fulfilment. Henry reads the reasoning as a warning against repetition — sabbath-breaking was one of the sins for which God had already brought judgements upon them, so that if they would not take warning but returned to the same sins, they had reason to expect further judgements.
18:
The argument from history is put as a question, and the commentators read it as naming a cause rather than drawing a parallel. Gill glosses the opening clause simply, that the fathers had profaned the sabbath in like manner. Keil and Delitzsch set out the full reasoning: Nehemiah reminds the nobles how their forefathers by such acts had brought all this evil on the people and the city — meaning the misery of the former exile and the oppression they were living under — and then turns it to the present, that by profaning the sabbath they were only increasing the wrath already lying upon Israel. Henry reads it as a warning against repetition rather than a general lament: sabbath-breaking was one of the sins for which God had already brought judgements upon them, so that if they would not take warning but returned to the same sins, they had reason to expect more.

What the appeal presupposes is itself worth noting. Ellicott observes that it assumes the hearers' familiarity with the express prediction of Jeremiah and with its literal fulfilment, so the force of the question depends on their knowing both the threat and the event. The verse therefore works less as persuasion than as a reminder of something already conceded.

The remedy that follows is physical and immediate, and the witnesses describe the timing with care. Gill explains the idiom about the gates growing dark: the word means shaded, and as Jarchi takes it, when the shadows of the sabbath eve were stretched out over the gates — for the sabbath itself did not begin until sunset and the appearing of the stars, but before that, as the sun declined, the shadows of the houses and the surrounding mountains spread across them. Clarke puts the same point as a clock reading: after sunset on the Friday evening Nehemiah caused the gates to be shut and kept them shut through the whole sabbath. Keil and Delitzsch record the two-part order, that the gates be closed and that they not be opened again until after the sabbath.

Who was set to watch is the detail three witnesses stop on, and they agree about why. Clarke says plainly that Nehemiah could not trust the ordinary officers, and so set some of his own servants to watch the gates, that no one might enter for the purpose of traffic. Wesley gives the same reason more briefly, a diffidence in those to whom the keeping of the gates was committed. Ellicott notes that these servants appear several times in public duty and reads their use here as provisional — they keep out traffickers until the formal appointment of the Levitical guard a few verses later, after which they would be relieved.
20:
The merchants respond to the shut gates by camping outside them, and the witnesses treat the move as an evasion rather than a defeat. Keil and Delitzsch explain why it worked: egress from the city could not be refused to its own inhabitants, so the rest of the sabbath was broken outside the walls instead of inside them. Gill names the traders as the Tyrians particularly, lodging outside for one sabbath or two, unable to get in because of the strict watch, and hoping the Jews would come out to them and buy, even though their goods were not admitted within the city. Clarke puts it in a line — they exposed their wares for sale on the outside of the walls.

Ellicott reads the phrase about once or twice as the point at which Nehemiah's patience ran out, and identifies two things that provoked him: the unseemliness of the encampment itself, and the evidence it gave that the traders were merely waiting to evade the law. On that reading the second sabbath is what settles the matter, since a single night outside the gates might have been accident and two could not be.

Nehemiah's answer is a warning backed by a threat, and the witnesses render the threat concretely. Gill describes him as testifying against their continuance there and calling heaven and earth to witness what he would do if they did not depart. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the threatened action as driving them away by force, and note the unusual grammatical form of the participle, which occurs only here. Clarke makes it specific: I will imprison every man of you. Each of them records the result in the same words the verse uses — from that time forth they came no more on the sabbath — and Ellicott observes that the testimony in word together with the threat of forcible action effectually removed the evil.

What the episode shows about the reform is that it needed two stages rather than one. Shutting the gates stopped the traffic from entering but moved it to the wall, where it was equally a breach and rather more visible; only the direct confrontation with the traders ended it. Keil and Delitzsch summarise the sequence as Nehemiah putting an end to this misdemeanour also, which places it alongside the earlier abuses rather than treating it as a postscript to them.
22:
The last measure of the sabbath reform replaces Nehemiah's own servants with Levites, and the commentators explain both halves of the order. Gill takes the cleansing to be from all ceremonial uncleanness, so that they might be fit in a ceremonial sense to perform the duties of the office on the sabbath day. Wesley gives two reasons together: the work they were now set upon, though common in its nature, was holy in its design and had respect to the sabbath; and the day on which they were to do it was itself the sabbath, for the observation of which they were obliged to purify themselves. Ellicott reads the purification as undertaken for a sacred duty and adds a further dimension — not without reference to their past neglect, which required to be forgiven — and calls the whole arrangement a high tribute to the sabbath ordinance.

Why Levites rather than porters is the question the verse raises, and Wesley answers it directly: not daring to trust the common porters, Nehemiah committed the charge of the city gates on the sabbath days to the Levites, to whom the care of sanctifying the sabbath properly belonged. Keil and Delitzsch are more cautious about the wording, observing that the measure is so briefly narrated that it does not plainly appear what it consisted in, and that the meaning of the phrase about coming and keeping the gates is doubtful.

The verse closes with a second prayer, and it draws the chapter's most pointed defence of the man praying. Clarke takes up the charge directly: some have thought Nehemiah deals with God too much on the principle of merit. That he wished God to remember him for good is evident enough, Clarke grants — and who does not wish the same? But that he expected heaven because of his good deeds does not appear; indeed the concluding clause of this very verse proves the contrary, showing that he expected nothing from God except through the greatness of His mercy. Clarke ends with an exclamation at those who, with that evidence before them, brand this good man as a workmonger.

The other witnesses read the prayer in the same direction and find the plea for mercy the decisive word. Ellicott observes that here too Nehemiah commits his fidelity to the merciful estimate of God, and notices a change of tone: something in connection with the sabbath, or in his retrospect of his own conduct, gives this passing prayer a peculiar pathos of humility. Wesley draws out the implication of the appeal to mercy, that although Nehemiah mentioned his good deeds he did not rest his case upon them. Keil and Delitzsch simply record the two petitions as they stand, to be remembered concerning this also and to be spared according to the greatness of God's mercy, which keeps the second prayer parallel to the first while adding to it the word the first did not use.
23:
The last abuse is the one the chapter opened by legislating against, and Henry makes that circularity the point. This is one instance more of Nehemiah's zeal for purifying his countrymen as a peculiar people to God, and Henry notes what it shows about his use of power — that this, and not the enriching of himself, was what he aimed at. The complaint is not new: it had been made in Ezra's time and much had been done towards a reformation then. But when the unclean spirit is cast out, Henry observes, if a watchful eye is not kept upon him he will re-enter, and so he did here — although in Ezra's time those who had married strange wives were compelled to part with them.

Which nations are named matters, because they are not all forbidden on the same footing. Gill distinguishes them: Ashdod, called Azotus elsewhere, was one of the five cities of the Philistines, who were none of the seven nations with whom marriage was expressly forbidden, so that marrying there was very unfit and improper rather than unlawful outright; whereas marriage with Ammonites and Moabites was unlawful. He also suggests how the Philistine connection arose in the first place — Ashdod was a mart of the Arabians, where they sold their goods and to which Jews might resort, and so be ensnared into such marriages.

Keil and Delitzsch read the grammar of the verse as describing a visitation rather than a chance discovery. It is not said that Nehemiah saw Jews, they point out, but the Jews who had brought home Ashdodite, Ammonite and Moabite wives; and from that definite construction Bertheau rightly infers that what Nehemiah found at this time was an established group rather than isolated offenders. They head the whole section with its outcome — marriages with foreign wives dissolved — which treats the episode as the last of the chapter's reforms rather than merely the last of its complaints.

Ellicott reads the evidence the other way and reaches a different estimate of scale. The punishment, he argues, shows that these were exceptional cases; but the transgression was of the most flagrant kind, since it was precisely the law read aloud at the chapter's opening that these marriages broke. The two readings are not easily reconciled: on one the offence was widespread enough to be found as a settled population, on the other it was rare enough that individual men could be singled out for punishment — and the chapter gives grounds for both, naming a class of offenders and then describing the chastisement of certain of them.
24:
The sign of the marriages is what the children sounded like. Ellicott identifies the mixture precisely, as Philistine and Aramaic. Gill notes where they picked it up, namely from their mothers. Keil and Delitzsch render the clause so that the weight falls on a positive loss rather than on the blending: the children could not speak the Jews' language at all, but spoke according to the tongue of each people. On that rendering what the verse reports is not an accent but an incapacity.

Clarke reconstructs the household that would produce such a result, and his account is the fullest any witness offers. Children were born in one family to Jewish and to Philistine mothers alike; the Jewish mother would always address hers in Hebrew or Chaldee, so they learnt those, while the Ashdod mother would always address hers in her own, so they learnt that. His conclusion is stark — under one roof were children who could not understand each other, one part using one tongue and the other part another. He supports the picture from domestic custom: the wives had separate apartments, and children of different wives did not ordinarily mingle.

Gill preserves a second construction of the word rendered half, and it alters what is being counted. Referred to the speech, it yields a mixed idiom, partly Jewish and partly Philistine. But some, he reports, refer the term instead to the number of the offspring — that half of them, which Jarchi takes to mean many of them, used the Ashdod tongue, namely those who were most with their mothers and chiefly reared by them.

Between these constructions Clarke takes a side and says so. He judges his own account the better explanation, as against the view which intimates that one and the same child spoke a jargon, half Ashdod and half Hebrew. The dispute is therefore not over the fact of the marriages but over what the clause measures: whether the corruption appears inside each child's speech, as a hybrid, or across the household, dividing one brother from another. Keil and Delitzsch carry the sentence straight on into Nehemiah's response without pausing over the question, which leaves the grammatical point to Gill and Clarke.
25:
Nehemiah's response is a series of acts rather than a single one, and what each act amounted to is reckoned differently. On the contending there is agreement: Gill has him argue with them, faithfully admonish and sharply reprove, and Clarke adds a formal setting, that he proved the fact against these iniquitous fathers in a legal assembly. On the cursing there are three readings. Clarke takes it as denouncing the judgements of God and the sentence of the law upon them. Wesley takes it as a sentence actually executed — he caused them to be excommunicated and cast out of the society of God's people. Ellicott takes it as neither threat nor sentence but citation: Nehemiah simply echoed the covenant sanction on this very point, which the people had themselves sworn to.

On the beating and the hair the comment turns to law and custom. Wesley grounds the stripes in the statute that regulated them, and limits them to those whose faults were most aggravated, treating this as a punishment added over and above the others. Clarke calls it whipping and the shaving a mark of the greatest ignominy. Wesley explains why it carried that force: the hair was an ensign of liberty among the eastern nations, and baldness a disgrace and a token of slavery. Ellicott notices who received it — some were selected for special punishment and humiliation — and sets beside it a telling parallel, that Ezra on a like occasion plucked off the hair of his own head, humbling himself where Nehemiah humbles the offenders. Keil and Delitzsch record the whole sequence without softening it: he contended with them, cursed them, smote certain of their men, and plucked off their hair.

Wesley also supplies the justification the severity needs, and it is a double one. These punishments were justly inflicted because the transgression was contrary both to a plain law of God and to the people's own late solemn covenants — so the offence was not only disobedience but perjury. The oath Nehemiah then exacts is read in the same light. Clarke describes it as binding them to make no intermarriages with those not of the seed of Israel; Ellicott, more exactly, says they were obliged to repeat the oath of the covenant they had already taken.

The argument Nehemiah reaches for is an example rather than a statute, and it is chosen for its weight. Gill states the case plainly: Solomon sinned by these very things, by marrying strange wives who drew him into idolatry. Ellicott draws out what the appeal assumes — that the language of Scripture concerning Solomon was familiar both to Nehemiah and to the transgressors — and calls it a remarkable instance of the faithful application of their own chronicles. The force of the comparison lies in the concessions the verse makes before it strikes: among many nations there was no king like Solomon, he was beloved of his God, and God made him king over all Israel; and yet even him did outlandish women cause to sin. If the best-placed man in the nation's history could not survive such marriages, the question that follows — whether Nehemiah should hearken to these men and let so great an evil pass — answers itself.
27:
The question Nehemiah puts to the offenders is a refusal dressed as an enquiry, and Gill supplies the sense of hearkening that makes it one: to hearken would be to suffer the thing to be done, to connive at it, and not to punish for it. Silence would have been complicity, so the question admits only one answer. Clarke turns the Solomon precedent around and aims it at the men in front of him — if God did not spare Solomon, who was so much beloved of Him, shall we spare you, who by your conduct are bringing down God's judgements upon Israel. The argument moves from the greater to the lesser twice over: from the king's standing to theirs, and from what God Himself did not withhold to what a governor may not.

At verse 28 the offence reaches the high priest's own house, and the commentators work out exactly whose house that is. Gill reads the man as a grandson of the high priest, taking the title in his version to attach to Eliashib rather than to Joiada his son, and records that Dr. Prideaux attaches it the other way. On the identification itself there is agreement: Gill and Clarke both follow Josephus in naming him Manasseh, brother of Jaddua the high priest and son of Joiada. Ellicott supplies the pattern the marriage completed. Eliashib was himself already allied by marriage to Tobiah; now one of his grandsons was brought into prominence as married to Sanballat. Both of Nehemiah's old adversaries had married their way into the priestly family, and the second match was the more conspicuous for following the first.

What Nehemiah did about it is read with a widening reach. Clarke keeps to the priestly register: he struck the man off the list of the priests and deemed him utterly unworthy of all connection and intercourse with truly religious people. Wesley lists the circles the man lost in turn — Nehemiah's own presence and court, the city and the temple, and the congregation and church of Israel. Ellicott puts it most briefly, that Nehemiah drove him into exile. Wesley then follows the exile to its consequence, again on Josephus: this was that Manasses who by Sanballat's interest procured liberty to build the Samaritan temple in mount Gerizim, and that sanctuary became the refuge of priests who had married strange wives or been otherwise criminal, and of others of the people in the same or like circumstances who went with them or after them.

Verse 29 hands the case over. Gill takes the prayer to ask that God remember the priests and punish them, their fault being that they defiled the priesthood by these marriages and rendered themselves unfit to officiate in it. Clarke reaches the same outcome by a different route, holding that God will remember their iniquities against them and punish them for their transgressions, but that Nehemiah's words are to be understood declaratively rather than as a wish. Ellicott draws the jurisdictional point, that this priestly violation of law is committed to God alone for punishment, and then grounds the charge of defilement: God chose the tribe of Levi for Himself and especially the house of Aaron, and every priest was to be holy to the Lord, which is what the covenant of the priesthood means — with a possible undertone of reference to the great covenant of chapter ten. Keil and Delitzsch read the verse forward instead, as the opening of the closing summary of all Nehemiah had effected for the community.
30:
The last two verses are a reckoning rather than a narrative, and Ellicott names the form: a summary recapitulation of the special work Nehemiah had done since his return. Gill reads the cleansing as reaching both ranks of the community, people and priests alike, and as having a concrete demand behind it — the men were obliged either to put the foreign wives away or to leave the country. Ellicott adds what the language of cleansing implies beyond the discipline already described, that there was doubtless some formal service of expiation to close the matter. Keil and Delitzsch set the clause inside the whole closing summary, where Nehemiah states that he cleansed them from all strangers and appointed the services for the priests and the Levites, each man in his own business, together with the wood offering at its appointed times and the firstfruits. On their reading the strangeness in question is foreign heathen custom, and chiefly these marriages.

The wood offering looks like a detail of housekeeping and is treated as anything but. Gill sets out the arrangement: Levites were appointed to receive the wood as it was brought, at the times and by the persons already fixed for it, to lay it up in its proper place, and to carry it to the altar when it was wanted. Clarke explains why so practical a provision earns a place in the final sentence of the book. It was a most necessary regulation, since without it the temple service could not have gone forward at all, and that is why Nehemiah names it among the most important services he had rendered to his nation.

The closing prayer is read as a plea for mercy rather than a claim on merit. Clarke is emphatic that remember me, O my God, for good has precisely the same meaning as O my God, have mercy upon me, and that it should be understood in that way alone. Wesley takes the same two words as a pattern for all praying, since for good may well be the summary of our petitions and we need no more than this to make us happy. Ellicott reads the words as an exit: with them Nehemiah leaves the scene, committing himself and his discharge of duty to the Righteous Judge. The committal was needed, on his account, because Nehemiah's conscientious fidelity had brought him into collision not only with external enemies but with many of his own brethren, and because his rigorous reformation has been assailed by moralists in every age — so he commits the whole case to God by anticipation.

Clarke closes with an estimate of the man. The Jews speak of Nehemiah as one of the greatest of their nation, and his concern for his country entitles him to the character of the first patriot that ever lived. Divine providence had made him a captive in Babylon, where his excellences were so apparent that the Persian king gave him the most respectable and confidential office in the whole court; yet the ease and affluence he enjoyed there he could not enjoy while his people were distressed, the sepulchres of his fathers trodden under foot, the altars of his God overturned, and His worship neglected or corrupted. He was willing to sacrifice wealth, ease, safety and life itself to restore the desolations of Israel, and God, seeing that desire, granted it. Clarke notes that several have therefore read him as a type of Christ, and that his own earlier notes clear him of mercenary views and of any religion grounded on human merit. Ellicott observes that with these words the annals of Old Testament history end; Clarke adds that the Jewish canon counts Ezra and Nehemiah as one book, and that the Syriac version closes with a colophon numbering its verses at two thousand three hundred and sixty-one.
